result:
For six years, I was responsible for turning off the stars.

It was less impressive than it sounds. There was a switch behind the planetarium desk, beside a kettle that tasted faintly of pennies. At five fifteen, after the last school group had gone, I shut down the projector, checked beneath the seats for jumpers and water bottles, and made the universe safe for the cleaners.

The stars did not disappear all at once. First went the faint ones. Then the familiar shapes unraveled. Orion lost his belt. The Great Bear became an argument about dots. Finally there was only the emergency exit sign, offering its modest green alternative to eternity.

I liked that part best.

People assumed I loved astronomy. I had put “enthusiastic amateur astronomer” on the application because my sister said employers wanted evidence of passion. Mostly I wanted a job I could walk to.

By my second year, though, I could find my way around the sky. I knew which facts made children gasp and which made their teachers check the time. Black holes were dependable. Distances were harder. Tell someone a star is four hundred light-years away and they nod politely. Tell them its light began traveling before their grandmother’s grandmother was born and sometimes they look up again.

The cleaner was called June. She arrived while I was putting the ticket money in the safe, dragging a vacuum cleaner with one wheel that refused to turn.

“Anything good up there today?” she would ask.

“Saturn.”

“Again?”

“It remains popular.”

June had cleaned the planetarium for eleven years without seeing a show. Her shift began when ours ended, and she said she wasn’t coming into work on her day off just to sit in the dark.

One wet November evening, the vacuum gave a cough and stopped.

June kicked it once, without conviction.

“That’s that,” she said.

I offered to ring maintenance.

“They’ll tell me to check the plug.”

“Have you?”

She looked at me.

While she filled in the fault report, I switched the projector back on. I was testing a new program for a group booked the following morning, but June put down her pen.

“Oh,” she said.

The stars sharpened above us.

She stood in the aisle with the vacuum hose still in her hand. Then she sat in the nearest seat.

I began explaining the winter constellations.

“No,” she said gently. “Just leave it a minute.”

So I did.

The projector hummed. Rain tapped somewhere beyond the dome. After a while I sat down too.

June watched for nearly ten minutes. When she got up, she folded the fault report into quarters and tucked it under the dead machine’s handle.

“My husband used to know all those,” she said.

I waited.

“Or said he did. Could’ve been making it up. I never checked.”

After that, we had an arrangement. On Fridays, before she started cleaning, I gave her ten minutes of sky.

Sometimes she asked for a particular place.

“What would it look like from Sydney?”

“Tonight?”

“June 1983.”

The computer could do that. It could put us almost anywhere, almost anywhen. Sydney, June 1983. Lisbon on her honeymoon. The village where she grew up, on a date she had written down on the back of a shopping receipt.

I never asked what had happened on those days. Once, when she requested an afternoon, I explained that there wouldn’t be much to see.

“I know,” she said. “Can you do it anyway?”

We sat beneath a pale blue dome.

In my sixth year, the council announced a refurbishment. The old projector would be replaced by a digital system. There would be reclining seats, interactive exhibits, a café serving things on wooden boards.

My job would become a visitor engagement role.

I could apply for it, they said.

Around the same time, my sister offered me work in her printing business. Better money. Regular hours. She needed someone who could be trusted to notice when an invitation said “pubic celebration.”

I took it.

On my last Friday, June arrived carrying two paper cups of tea from the bakery.

“Not drinking that kettle water,” she said. “Not on an occasion.”

We sat in the middle row.

“Where do you want to go?” I asked.

She thought about it.

“Here.”

“What date?”

“Now.”

I entered our location and the time. Above us appeared the sky we would have seen if the dome, the roof, and the November clouds had been removed.

For once, I didn’t recognize it immediately. There were always constellations I neglected: faint, awkward arrangements that never featured in the school show. I found one and tried to remember its name.

June leaned back, holding her tea with both hands.

“Will you miss it?”

“Some of it.”

She nodded.

We stayed until her phone alarm went off. She had other buildings to clean.

I shut down the projector. We watched the stars disappear in their usual order. Then June collected our cups, and I went to clear out my desk.

Outside, she was wrestling the vacuum into the back of her car.

“They fixed the wheel,” I said.

“Eventually.”

I helped her lift it over the lip of the boot. The machine was heavier than I expected.

June drove off. I stood beneath the streetlamp, looking for my keys, then remembered I had left the building keys on the desk, as instructed. It would take a few days to stop checking for them.

On the walk home, I passed the bakery, the closed pharmacy, the bus shelter with its cracked panel. A light rain started. I put up my hood.

Near my flat, I stopped to let a man maneuver a sofa through a doorway. He was arguing with someone I couldn’t see.

Above the rooftops was one bright point. Jupiter, probably, though I wasn’t certain.

I waited for another to appear.

Then the man asked if I could hold the door, and I said yes.
